title: Extension points and maintainable classes
idea: An extensible design adds a feature by writing new code at a planned extension point; a maintainable one keeps each change small, local and easy to read.
points: Find the axis that keeps changing, like pricing rules, and put an interface there.
The core depends on that interface and never names a concrete rule.
A new rule is a new class plus one line of wiring.
Small classes with one reason to change are cheaper to read, test and fix.

hero.title: Adding a rule without touching the core

edges.label: implements
edges.caption: Each existing rule implements the interface and holds its own pricing logic.

edges.label: implements
edges.caption: A new delivery option: one new class and one line in `main`. `Shipping` is not edited or retested.

code.title: One extension point
code.caption: Three delivery rules behind one interface. `LockerRule` arrived later and needed no edit to `Shipping`.

walk.text: The extension point: a name, a price, and an optional `appliesTo` filter.
A `default` method gives rules a sensible answer, so a rule that always applies can skip it.
The core filters and prices through the interface; it holds a copied, unmodifiable list.
Each rule is a few lines and has one reason to change.
The new feature is a new class; existing code stays as it was.
Wiring is the only shared line that changed.

pitfalls: Do not add extension points for changes nobody expects; each one costs reading time.
A growing `switch` on a type code is a missing extension point; replace it.
Keep wiring in one place, so adding a rule does not scatter edits.

quiz.q: What does this print, using the same three rules?
quiz.why: Standard always applies: 300 + 4.0 × 100 = 700. Express allows up to 5 kg, and `toLocker` is true. The list keeps wiring order.

takeaway: Put one interface where change keeps coming, and keep everything else small.
